title: Cyrus and the Room
premise: Freya Eriksen, a meticulous property surveyor, is hired to appraise a derelict farmhouse whose measurements refuse to stay constant — and whose basement well seems to appraise her back. When her overnight sleep-recording device captures a second voice answering questions she never asked aloud, she discovers the house belongs to the memory of a girl taken in 1974 and never found. As Freya's documentation becomes communion, she learns the house demands not an appraisal but a restitution: what was stolen in 1974 must be returned before the well refills on the winter solstice. In the end, Freya chooses love over duty — returning the girl's remains and the truth of who took them, at the cost of her career and nearly her life — and the house finally lets its measurements rest.
about_author: Paloma Zhou is a former building inspector from coastal Maine who spent a decade writing survey reports before turning to fiction. Her work explores how places keep accounts, and what it costs to balance them.

chapters.title: The Square Footage of Grief
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She arrives at the Aldous farmhouse for a routine estate appraisal, noting odd details: doorways off by inches between visits, a cold draft rising from a sealed well cap. Emotional beat: professional detachment beginning to crack as the house resists being measured.

chapters.title: Inventory
chapters.summary: Freya documents every room, photographing a child's shoebox hidden behind plaster that contains a hair ribbon and a 1974 newspaper clipping about a missing girl, Maren Voss. Beat: curiosity sharpening into unease; she pockets the clipping against protocol.

chapters.title: Appraisal Back
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Her laser measure returns different numbers each pass; the floor plan she drafts redraws itself overnight. A neighbor warns her the house 'was never sold, only lent.' Beat: the first undeniable wrongness, dread taking root.

chapters.title: The Recorder
chapters.summary: Unable to sleep on-site, Freya leaves her audio recorder running. Playback captures her own sleep-talk — and a second voice, young and patient, answering questions she never asked. Beat: terror braided with a terrible tenderness toward the voice.

chapters.title: Questions in the Dark
chapters.summary: Freya begins asking questions aloud before sleeping. The voice — Maren — answers in fragments: a name half-spoken, 'he said it was for the well,' a date. Beat: intimacy forming across fifty years; Freya realizes documentation has become prayer.

chapters.title: Duty Calls
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, intercut with her firm's pressure to finalize the appraisal for a developer buyer. Her supervisor dismisses the discrepancies; her report deadline looms. Beat: the squeeze between professional obligation and the truth accumulating in her recordings.

chapters.title: The Voss File
chapters.summary: Freya visits county archives and meets elderly records clerk Halvard, who remembers 1974: Maren vanished during the solstice; her father was suspected but never charged; the well was searched and sealed. Beat: grief for a justice that never arrived.

chapters.title: What the Well Keeps
chapters.summary: Night. The voice leads Freya — via recorded instructions played back — to the well cap, which is now warm. She dreams of descending and wakes with wet shoes and silt on her cuffs. Beat: the house has begun moving her; agency eroding.

chapters.title: A Man Named Aldous
chapters.summary: Halvard's POV chapter. He recalls Edmund Aldous, the father: a man hollowed by debt who 'sold something' the week Maren disappeared. Halvard confesses he burned a page of the 1974 file out of loyalty. Beat: guilt compounding; the past insisting on testimony.

chapters.title: Second Voice, First Lie
chapters.summary: Freya catches an inconsistency: Maren's voice describes a brother who, per records, never existed. The house's rooms now rearrange around her while she watches. Beat: realization that the house curates memory — some of what it shows is bait.

chapters.title: The Developer
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The buyer's representative arrives, eager, and stands too long over the open well cap. Freya falsifies nothing but delays the report, sabotaging her own standing. Beat: duty and conscience openly at war; first real cost paid.

chapters.title: Ribbon and Ring
chapters.summary: In the wall cavity, Freya finds a wedding ring engraved E.A. — Edmund's — wrapped in Maren's ribbon. The recorder captures Maren saying, 'He put me where he put his promises.' Beat: horror crystallizing into comprehension of what was taken.

chapters.title: Refill
chapters.summary: Water sounds rise through the house at night; the well is refilling ahead of the solstice. Maren's voice grows fainter, more distant, as if sinking. Beat: a ticking clock made audible; urgency replaces fear.

chapters.title: Confession Tape
chapters.summary: Freya leaves the recorder by the well; morning playback holds a man's voice — Edmund's — mid-confession, naming an accomplice still alive: his old hired hand, now a respected retired judge. Beat: justice outside the law becomes possible, and necessary.

chapters.title: The Judge's House
chapters.summary: Freya confronts Judge Rennick, who denies everything until she plays the tape. He breaks: they hid Maren in the dry well when she threatened to expose their fraud, and sealed it. Beat: revulsion and cold clarity; the law itself was the accomplice.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Freya catalogs the takings: Maren's life, her name, the ribbon, the ring, the truth. She understands the house wants all of it returned — publicly, physically, before the solstice. Beat: resolve hardening into ritual purpose.

chapters.title: Deadline
chapters.summary: Her firm terminates her for the delayed report; her apartment lease ends; she moves into the farmhouse deliberately. Beat: love against duty resolved — she chooses the dead girl over her own standing.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Solstice eve. Freya opens the well cap and descends with rope and light, the water already at her knees, guided by Maren's voice growing stronger below. Beat: claustrophobic climax approach; courage as devotion.

chapters.title: The Room Below
chapters.summary: Climax. At the bottom, a dry room the surveys could never find: Maren's remains, the ribbon's pair, and Edmund's ledger of debts. Rennick arrives to stop her; the well begins filling in earnest. Freya chooses the ledger and the bones over the ladder. Beat: sacrifice at full price.

chapters.title: Returned
chapters.summary: Freya surfaces with the remains as Rennick is taken by the collapsing stair — the well keeps him. She lays Maren's bones in the churchyard at dawn, ribbon and ring atop them, and reads the ledger aloud to witnesses. Beat: restitution completed; grief transfigured into ceremony.

chapters.title: Final Measurement
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She surveys the house one last time: every measurement exact, stable, ordinary. The recorder plays only silence — then, once, a small voice saying thank you. Beat: release; the house's accounts closed.

chapters.title: Paloma's Note
chapters.summary: Epilogue framed as Freya's final document: her resignation letter, the corrected appraisal valuing the house at exactly what was lost, and a last line — 'Some properties are held in trust by the dead.' Beat: quiet, haunted peace; documentation fulfilled as prayer.
